title: Finding a way, and still becoming
summary: There is a familiar way of describing solo mothers: strong, resilient, self-sacrificing. But while these words are often meant as compliments, even these positive labels can sometimes become a kind…

blocks.text: There is a familiar way of describing solo mothers: strong, resilient, self-sacrificing. But while these words are often meant as compliments, even these positive labels can sometimes become a kind of box, reducing a woman’s story only to what she has endured rather than who she is, what she wants, and who she is still becoming. It is this space between identity and possibility that globally acclaimed Brazilian photographer Angélica Dass explores in “100 Portraits of Becoming,” TECNO’s two-year global storytelling initiative that brings together 100 real people and their evolving personal stories across Kenya, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Brazil, and the Philippines.

Dass has spent much of her career questioning the assumptions people make based on appearance, identity and skin color. It is this long-standing interest in representation that makes Dass a natural collaborator for ‘100 Portraits of Becoming.’

“100 Portraits of Becoming is an amazing opportunity, because I get to meet and have conversations with so many people all over the globe. It’s a project about meetings. When you think about the word becoming you think of the moment of transformation. Each time I learn about a new story, it transforms the way that I see this person, people who are similar, and I can see their culture, too. So, becoming is the transformation that we experience when we meet each other. We are becoming all the time, we are changing, we are being transformed,” Dass expressed.
Her-story in the making

For the campaign’s Philippines chapter, Dass turned her lens toward Filipino solo mothers and the people who form part of their everyday world. What emerged was not simply a montage of stories about hardship, but a more nuanced look at how these women navigate changing circumstances, making choices, adapting, asking for help, and finding ways to keep moving forward.

Dass considers this an important distinction because at the heart of these stories is a question that feels particularly relevant in the Philippines: beyond what she has gone through, who is she, and how is she still becoming?

For her, a woman may be a solo mother, but she can also be a professional, daughter, friend, student, athlete, content creator or a community builder. Motherhood may be central to her life, but it does not necessarily erase the other dimensions of her identity.

blocks.caption: Internationally recognized photographer Angelica Dass captures a solo mom using the TECNO CAMON Slim 5G.

blocks.text: The process of becoming is also about children who carry their mothers’ lessons forward, and about grandparents, relatives and friends who quietly become part of the ‘village’. It is about people who learn, adapt, ask for help and find a way. This is where the Filipino concept of diskarte (resourcefulness) enters the conversation.

Diskarte, in this context, is about finding a way. “What I heard in these stories was about finding a way, adapting, using limited resources, asking for help, making choices and making something workable,” Dass shared. “Diskarte is also deeply connected with my own Brazilian roots. The word may be Filipino, but the experience is universal because everywhere life is hard and we have to find a way to make it lighter”.
The Village and Mutual Care

Being a solo mother does not necessarily mean she has to do things alone. The way Dass sees it, they are surrounded by a community filled with people they can trust. And this principle defines Twinkle Dimayuga Zamora’s story.

Rather than trying to become a superwoman and carry all the burdens alone, Twinkle reached out to friends and learned to ask for help. In fact, she helped build MAMA, a community supporting solo mothers through parenting and grief support, self-care and legal guidance. “I learned to ask for a village. Now I’m building one for others,” Zamora proudly said. Her experience offers perhaps the clearest reminder that asking for help can also be diskarte.

blocks.caption: Twinkle Dimayuga Zamora photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: Support systems also form an essential part of these portraits. Such is the case of Mark Joseph Robis, who cared for his cousin while the child’s single mother worked abroad. Their arrangement became part of a wider family relationship built on reciprocity. Years earlier, she had helped care for him and supported his education. Now, that care has come full circle. “In our family, care always finds its way home,” he said, challenging the assumption that distance equates to absence.

blocks.caption: Mark Joseph Robis photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: Zamora and Robis’ stories are similarly reflected in content creator Jessica Rose “Nanay Jecka” Tinio’s. Her grandmother had raised a family on her own, and when her mother later became a solo mother and worked abroad, the grandmother stepped in to help care for the family.

blocks.caption: Jessica Rose “Nanay Jecka” Tinio photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: “It’s not just function, it’s community,” Dass emphasized.
Uncompromised Ambition

A mother’s strength can also serve as a blueprint for personal fulfillment. A case in point, breadwinner Ely Haig refuses to let her identity be redefined solely on her role as a solo mother. Instead, she balances family responsibilities with her passion as a padel player because for her, motherhood was never about compromising your ambitions, it’s about expanding her identity and capacity as a person. “Motherhood added to who I am. It never had to replace who I was,” she said.

blocks.caption: Ely Haig photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: This same spirit of ambition is also seen in the journey of Eunice Angeles, a fourth-year nursing student raised by a Qatar-based solo mother. “People saw what was missing. My mother showed me how to find a way, and now I find my own,” she beamed.

blocks.caption: Eunice Angeles photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: That adaptability spans generations in the story of content creator Jessica Rose “Nanay Jecka” Tinio. Her grandmother had raised a family on her own, and when her mother later became a solo mother and worked abroad, the grandmother stepped in to help care for the family.

The stories in 100 Portraits of Becoming complement that idea by showing both advocacy and context. The women find ways forward, but their ability to adapt does not mean every burden should be theirs to solve individually. A mother’s diskarte may solve an immediate problem, but it can also shape how a child understands possibility tomorrow.

“We don’t romanticize their struggles at all. In front of the camera, I see beauty, power; I see people who love themselves and this is what I want to show in my images. There is such amount of human suffering, stereotyping, and what we want to really show is the celebration of who they are. This is something that I am really happy to do. Everybody in front of my camera are proud, happy, shining, confident and comfortable,” Dass said.
When technology becomes a tool to break labels

Society quickly categories people based on first impressions, and these impressions can easily turn into lasting stereotypes. To dismantle them, we need a different approach—an approach that captures the full depth of a person’s story. This is where technology steps in to not simplify the reality, but to reveal it.

In 100 Portraits of Becoming, the camera is therefore not simply documenting what someone looks like. It becomes a way of asking the viewer to pause before categorizing, to look again, and see the person before and beyond the label.

The fascinating second layer of this project is that the portraits were created using TECNO’s CAMON Slim 5G. For a photographer of Dass’s stature, choosing a smartphone over the traditional professional camera could easily become the story. But she sees it differently. “The CAMON Slim 5G is a tool,” she shared. “TECNO gave me a tool to do what I do best, and that’s taking pictures, connecting with human beings, doing portraits.” Technology, in her own words, does not replace the photographer’s vision; instead, it enables it.

blocks.caption: Photographer Angelica Dass using the TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: It is important to note that CAMON Slim 5G’s Universal Tone technology is designed to represent a wider spectrum of human skin tones more accurately. “We also brought our cameras and other gadgets, but I found that it is easier to take pictures with a phone, and the colors are amazing! For someone like me—a woman with an African descent, someone that belongs south of the planet—being able to try this technology is something that can help us,” she affirmed.

For this project, CAMON Slim 5G was more than just a device, it embodied the campaign’s message. As Dass pointed out, technology is only ever a tool, and it’s used to showcase human connection. TECNO extended this idea by choosing working women, particularly single working mothers, as the emotional lens of 100 Portraits of Becoming.

These women represent the brand’s philosophy, ‘Make it Lighter,’ because of the diskarte they display that keeps families afloat—from balancing work, caregiving, managing finances, and deciding what’s best for the family.

The CAMON Slim 5G, with its slim design and Universal Tone camera, reflects that same principle. It lightens their load and captures them not only as mothers, but as women with their own dreams and stories and as women becoming.
The bigger picture

Perhaps that is where TECNO’s ‘Make it Lighter’ brand philosophy finds its most natural place in the story. Making life lighter does not mean pretending life is easy; a smartphone cannot solve the realities of solo parenthood, and it can never replace family, community or government support. For Dass and other visual storytellers, technology can help make creative expression more immediate and accessible.

blocks.caption: Photographer Angelica Dass captures a moment with a campaign participant using the TECNO CAMON Slim 5G.

blocks.text: At its core, TECNO is a technology brand built around possibility. TECNO’s technology simply enters that story as one more tool in the hands of people who are already finding ways to move forward.

“When we think about ‘becoming’ as transformation, we should also think about ways we can become who we want to be. So, if I can share something that I learned from this project, it is this: ‘becoming’ is also trying to find ways to be you,” Dass concluded.

The Philippines chapter of 100 Portraits of Becoming resonates beyond the stories of solo mothers themselves. It asks audiences to reconsider the labels they place on other people as well as the labels they place on themselves.
One hundred portraits. One hundred stories. One hundred ways of seeing humanity, not as categories, not with labels, but as real people in the process of becoming.
